sentences.text: Duriavenator was a large theropod dinosaur estimated to reach lengths of 5 to 7 meters and weigh approximately one ton.
Its skull contained about four teeth in the premaxilla, 14 to 16 in the maxilla, and 14 to 15 in the lower jaw.
A distinctive feature of this animal is a prominent palatal process on the premaxilla, which is more developed than in other basal tetanurans.
The maxilla also displays eleven foramina, roughly 2 mm in diameter, on its surface that connect with the premaxilla.
Additionally, two pneumatic chambers are visible in the corner of the antorbital fossa within the maxilla.
Research from 2009 noted that the front teeth were longer than the rear ones, circular in cross-section, and inclined forward.
Skull bones and teeth were collected by Edward Cleminshaw from the Inferior Oolite near Greenhill, close to Sherborne in Dorset, in 1882.
Further collection of upper and lower jaw bones occurred near Sherborne in the same year.
In 1883, Richard Owen initially classified these fossils as belonging to Megalosaurus bucklandii.
The specimen was recognized as a distinct species by 1964 and formally described as Megalosaurus hesperis in 1974.
Roger B. J. Benson later moved the species to its own genus, Duriavenator, in 2008.
In 2016, Paul suggested that megalosaurids like Duriavenator were ambush predators that hunted sauropods and stegosaurs.
In 2017, Rothschild and Naples hypothesized that lateral grooves on Duriavenator's dentary functioned as sensory organs analogous to fish lateral lines.
The genus Duriavenator was officially established by Benson in 2008.
The specific name hesperis was originally applied by Waldman in 1974.
In 2008, researchers confirmed that Duriavenator belongs to the group Tetanurae.
Phylogenetic analyses from 2010 onwards indicate that Duriavenator is part of the family Megalosauridae and ranks among the oldest tetanuran theropods.
Shared unique characteristics confirm that Duriavenator was a member of the clade Tetanurae and specifically the family Megalosauridae.
Duriavenator lived during the Middle Jurassic, approximately between 171 and 167 million years ago, within the Bajocian stage.
Fossils of this animal date specifically to the Bajocian stage.
It is known from the Upper Inferior Oolite Formation, a geological layer of Bajocian age.
During the Middle Jurassic, Britain was situated in the subtropics and formed part of an island archipelago.

Waldman suggested that Duriavenator may have possessed five premaxillary tooth sockets, a trait that would make it unique among megalosauroids, though this number cannot be directly observed in the specimen.
The species name hesperis refers to Hesperia, a region British authors associated with Great Britain or West Dorset.
